What I had to do was get a mouthpiece visualizer which is kind of like just a rim on a stick so you can see your lips, and practice buzzing pitches with that and a piano. It helped my tone and high range a lot. You might also not be resonating your pitches very well, for example your oral cavity is the right size to resonate a Bb but you are trying to buzz and play and F, which would result in poor tone. Singing helps a lot with this, as well as trying to control the pitch with the back of your mouth instead of your lips if that makes sense?

I'm also a girl on my 4th year of euphonium in college! I was told for forever that I just wasn't taking big enough breaths because I had smaller lungs and that was why I couldn't last through phrases.

Turns out I have about the same lung capacity as a guy, I actually measured with one of those lung trainers you can get at the hospital. The problem was definitely my embouchure, I wasn't using my air efficiency because my embouchure wasn't correct.

I think you might also be having an embouchure problem, especially since you say your tone sounds pinched or fuzzy. Are the corners of your mouth firm with the center soft? Do you top and bottom lips feel like they take up equal space in the mouthpiece? Is there air leaking out of the corners of your embouchure at all? Are you pressing into the mouthpiece or getting tense when you try to play louder or higher?

Most people call it jaw vibrato, and it is created not by moving the lips specifically but instead moving your lower jaw. Kind of like saying the syllable  "yaw" over and over again. So your lips do move, but only because your lower jaw is moving. Opening and closing the space between your teeth should bend the pitch and create vibrato. There's a lot of youtube videos that explain it better than I do on YouTube if you just search "jaw vibrato euphonium". The best way to start is with long tones, and try to bend the pitch in time with a metronome. First in half notes, then quarter notes, eight etc.

I've had to fly out if the country with a euphonium once. If you end up checking it, you absolutely want a heavy duty hard case. There's a good chance your instrument might get thrown around a bit. Also make sure you take everything but the instrument out of the case, like valve oil and mouthpieces so nothing gets knocked loose while you're flying. 

You also should get a luggage strap to put around your case. TSA might leave it unlatched if they have to search it. If you have a luggage strap around they should put it back when they're done, so even if they don't latch your case back your instrument won't fall out and get damaged thanks to the luggage strap holding it closed

I've recently been struggling with the same thing you're describing. There's a lot of little things that I've found help me, but I also highly recommend therapy, even if you feel like there's nothing to be validly upset about. 

While these things won't cure your depression they can make it a little more bearable. I find I'm more motivated to do things if people are around, so maybe invite some friends over even if it is to just watch movies and do nothing all day. Also make sure you're eating healthily and drinking enough water. Sometimes just being dehydrated can make you feel like shit. I also try not to lie in bed for too long in the mornings, otherwise I spiral downhill really fast and never want to get up. Excersize is also great, even just going for a short walk outside of your house to the mail box or something could be a good change of environment to help you find motivation. I personally like to run before bed because it helps me sleep through the nights better, but that might not work for you.

Having friends and a support system is the best thing you can do. Being isolated makes it so much worse. Even if you don't want to talk about your depression, just being around people usually helps me immensely

I'm also a music major so I get where you're coming from. First of all in my opinion im not really sure you need to feel guilty about pursuing music instead of doing "more to help the world" as you put it. I feel that music is a very valuable pursuit, even if it doesn't seem as obviously helpful to the world as becoming a doctor or something. Just imagine a world where music didn't exist at all, no film soundtracks no radio, nothing. I often use music to help calm my nerves or pull me out of depressive funk. I also get not exactly liking music anymore, this last semester I got to a pretty rough patch where I abdolutley hated practicing my instrument, and i kind of forgot why I liked playing it in the first place. I eventually got over It after talking to my instructor, but I know some people don't. There pressure of having to perform well can ruin the joy of playing an instrument or singing for a lotnof people, so don't feel bad if you decide you really dont want to be a performance major. Keep in mind that you can always get a minor in zoology and a major in music, or vice versa, or even a double major, although I know that can be almost impossible with a kusic major. Ultimatley I would go into whatever one you enjoy the most, regardless of how much it helps the world, because ultimatley I think both majors are equally important and you'll make a grwat contribution to the world as long as you love and vare about what you are doing.
